std.how_it_works: Computes the standard deviation of the values of an array, along the specified axis — it measures the dispersion of the data around the mean.
std.name: Standard Deviation

output.result: Computed standard deviation.

std.usage_tips: By default it computes the population standard deviation (ddof=0); use ddof=1 for the sample standard deviation (division by N−1). `axis=0` gives one value per variable, the basis of autoscaling.

subtracao.description: Subtraction A − B, element by element.
subtracao.how_it_works: Subtracts B from A (A − B) element by element. The shapes must be equal or compatible by broadcasting.
subtracao.name: Subtraction

output.result: Result of A - B, element by element.

subtracao.usage_tips: With broadcasting, subtracting a mean vector from each row of X is equivalent to centering the data. Also useful for removing a reference/blank spectrum.

sum.how_it_works: Sums all the values of an array, along the specified axis.
sum.name: Sum

output.result: Computed sum.

sum.usage_tips: Use `axis` to sum in one direction (axis=0: total of each variable; axis=1: total of each sample). In spectra, summing over the spectral axis gives the total intensity of each sample — the basis of an area normalization.

svd.historical_note: The singular value decomposition theorem goes back to independent work by Eugenio Beltrami and Camille Jordan in the 1870s — long before any computational application existed.
svd.how_it_works: Decomposes any matrix X into three matrices: U (left singular vectors), Σ (singular values, in decreasing order of importance) and Vᵀ (right singular vectors), such that X = U·Σ·Vᵀ. It is the mathematical operation behind PCA — the squared singular values are proportional to the explained variance.

input.A: Input matrix, any shape (does not need to be square).

svd.name: SVD (Singular Value Decomposition)
svd.usage_tips: Outputs: U, S (singular values, in decreasing order) and Vt. With `full_matrices=false` (default) the computation is economical. For centered data, the scores of a PCA are U·S and the loadings are the rows of Vt — but for exploratory analysis the `pca` block already delivers everything ready.

svm.description: Support Vector Machine with RBF or linear kernel.
svm.historical_note: Formalized by Vladimir Vapnik and Corinna Cortes in 1995, based on the statistical learning theory Vapnik had been developing since the 1960s.
svm.how_it_works: Finds the decision boundary that maximizes the margin between classes. For data that are not linearly separable in the original space, it uses a kernel (RBF is the most common) that projects the data into a higher-dimensional space where linear separation becomes possible, without having to compute that projection explicitly (the "kernel trick").

output.metrics_cal: Classification metrics on calibration: accuracy and balanced accuracy.
output.model: Metadata of the trained SVM model (type and main hyperparameters).
output.support_vectors: Training samples that define the decision boundary (support vectors).

params.C: Regularization parameter (the larger, the less tolerant of classification error).

svm.usage_tips: It tends to perform well even with few samples and many variables (a common scenario in spectroscopy), but it is sensitive to data scale — always normalize/autoscale before training.

tensor_random_forest.description: Random Forest on an unfolded tensor.

tensor_regression.description: Tensor regression with the weight coefficient in CP format.

tensor_svd.description: Higher-Order SVD for exploratory analysis of tensors.

terceira_ordem.description: Third-order calibration for fourth-order analytical data.

trace.description: Sum of the main-diagonal elements. Requires a square A.
trace.how_it_works: Computes the trace of a square matrix — the sum of the main-diagonal elements.
trace.name: Matrix Trace

output.result: Trace of the matrix.

trace.usage_tips: The sum of the eigenvalues equals the trace. For a covariance matrix, the trace is the total variance of the data — the denominator of the variance explained per component in PCA.

transformer.description: Transformer with multi-head attention for spectral series.
transformer.historical_note: Introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017 ("Attention Is All You Need"), originally for machine translation — it is now the basis of large language models, and has also been adapted to spectral signals.
transformer.how_it_works: Architecture based on an attention mechanism (self-attention): instead of processing the sequence point by point like the RNN, it directly computes how much each point of the spectrum "should pay attention" to every other point, capturing relationships between distant regions of the spectrum without needing recurrence.

input.y: Value to predict or class label.

output.history: Metrics of the last training epoch (e.g. loss and, if available, validation metrics).
output.model: Metadata of the trained Transformer model (type and main hyperparameters).

params.dense_units: Units of the final dense layers.

transformer.usage_tips: It is the most data- and compute-hungry architecture in the catalog — it only pays off with a considerable volume of training data; for small datasets, PLS or CNN-1D tend to generalize better.

transpose.description: Permutes the axes of the array.
transpose.how_it_works: Transposes (permutes) the axes of a matrix or N-way tensor — swaps rows and columns (or reorders the modes, in tensors).
transpose.name: Transpose / Axis Permutation

params.axes: New order of the axes (e.g. [1,0] to transpose a matrix). Omitted = reverses all axes.

transpose.usage_tips: Without giving `axes`, the order of the axes is reversed (in matrices, it swaps rows and columns). In tensors, `axes` defines the desired permutation — for example [1, 0, 2] swaps the first two modes.

tratamento_missing.description: Fills in or removes missing values (NaN).
tratamento_missing.how_it_works: Handles missing values (NaN) according to the strategy chosen in `strategy`: 'mean' or 'median' (fills with the column mean/median), 'zero' (fills with 0), 'interpolate' (linear interpolation along each row) or 'drop' (removes samples containing NaN). For more sophisticated imputation, see the 'Missing Data' family (still under development in this version).
tratamento_missing.name: Missing Value Handling

output.X_filled: Data after handling the missing values.

params.strategy: Strategy for filling in/removing missing values.

tratamento_missing.usage_tips: With 'drop', remember to remove the same samples from y. 'interpolate' makes sense for spectra (neighboring points are similar); 'mean'/'median' are more appropriate for independent variables. Always inspect how many NaN there were beforehand: filling in many values distorts the model.

tucker3.historical_note: Proposed by Ledyard Tucker in 1966, even before PARAFAC — it is the most direct multiway generalization of PCA (PCA is a special case of Tucker with a single mode).
tucker3.how_it_works: Decomposes an order-3 tensor into a smaller core plus three loading matrices, one per mode — unlike PARAFAC, it allows a different number of components per mode and captures interactions between components of different modes (through the core), but in exchange it has no unique solution.

output.core: Core tensor of the Tucker decomposition.
output.factors: List of loading matrices, one per mode.
output.fit: Quality of fit (1 - ||X - X_rec|| / ||X||), from 0 to 1.
output.model: Metadata: type and ranks per mode.

params.n_iter_max: Maximum number of iterations of the optimization algorithm.
params.ranks: Rank (number of components) in each of the 3 modes of the tensor — must have exactly 3 values.

tucker3.usage_tips: Use it instead of PARAFAC when there is no reason to expect exact trilinearity in the data, or when you want to explore how many components each mode really needs independently.

tucker_regression.description: Regression via Tucker decomposition: scores → linear regression.

u_pca.description: PCA on an unfolded tensor (multiway exploratory analysis).

u_pls.description: PLS on unfolded multiway data (unfold + PLS).
u_pls.how_it_works: Unfolds the input tensor into a 2D matrix (samples × all other flattened modes), normalizes each column (mean 0, standard deviation 1) and runs an ordinary PLS on it — simpler than a true N-PLS, but it loses the separation between the original modes.

input.X: Data tensor, order ≥ 3 — will be internally unfolded into a matrix before the PLS.

output.metrics_cal: Calibration metrics (fit on the training set itself): RMSEC, R2C and bias.
output.model: Metadata of the trained U-PLS model (type and main hyperparameters).
output.scores: Scores of the samples in the latent space (samples × components).

u_pls.usage_tips: Faster and simpler to interpret than N-PLS when the multilinear structure is not the focus — but if the different modes of the tensor have distinct physical meaning that you want to preserve in the model interpretation, prefer N-PLS.

unfolding.description: Turns an N-way tensor into a 2D matrix along one mode.
unfolding.how_it_works: Unfolds ("flattens") a higher-order tensor into a 2D matrix along a chosen mode — a necessary step before applying any technique that only accepts 2D input (e.g. ordinary PCA) to originally multiway data.

input.X: Array with 2 or more dimensions (N-way tensor) to be unfolded into a matrix.

unfolding.name: Unfolding (Tensor → Matrix)

output.X_unf: 2D matrix resulting from unfolding along the chosen mode.
output.mode: Mode used as the rows of the unfolding (the same `mode` parameter).
output.original_shape: Shape of the original tensor, needed to revert with `folding`.

unfolding.usage_tips: A typical step before applying PCA or PLS to multiway data. `mode` chooses which mode becomes the ROWS of the matrix (mode=0 keeps the samples as rows). Keep `original_shape` and `mode`: they are needed to undo the operation with `folding`.

unique.description: Returns the unique, sorted values of X. Equivalent to MATLAB's unique().
unique.how_it_works: Returns the unique (non-repeated) values of the array, sorted. It also returns the count of occurrences of each unique value — useful for analyzing the distribution of class labels.

input.X: 1D or N-D array (will be flattened internally).

unique.name: Unique Values

output.counts: Number of occurrences of each unique value.
output.result: Unique values, sorted.

unique.usage_tips: Use unique(y) to check which classes exist and how many samples each has before training a classification model. Class imbalance may call for balancing strategies.

unit_converter.description: Converts between spectral units: nm, cm⁻¹, eV, THz, µm.

var.description: Variance along an axis. Equivalent to MATLAB's var().
var.how_it_works: Computes the dispersion of the data around the mean — the mean of the squared deviations. With ddof=0 (default) it is the population variance; with ddof=1 it is the sample variance (division by N-1).

input.X: Input array whose squared standard deviation will be computed.

var.name: Variance

output.result: Variance computed along the chosen axis.

var.usage_tips: Use var(X) before scaling the data to understand how much each variable contributes to the total variance. var(X, axis=0) computes per column (per variable), axis=1 per row (per sample).

vip.historical_note: Formalized by Svante Wold and collaborators in the 1990s as a variable interpretation/selection tool specific to PLS models.
vip.how_it_works: Variable Importance in Projection: internally fits a PLS model (`n_components`) of y on X and computes, for each variable, its contribution to explaining y across all components (each component's weights are weighted by the variance of y it explains). Variables with VIP greater than or equal to `threshold` (default 1.0, a common rule of thumb) are selected.

output.model: Summary of the internal PLS used (technique and effective number of components).
output.selected_indices: Indices of the variables with VIP ≥ threshold.
output.threshold: VIP threshold used in the selection.
output.vip_scores: VIP score of each variable — values > 1 generally indicate a relevant variable.

params.n_components: Number of PLS components used to compute the VIP.
params.threshold: VIP threshold above which the variable is considered important (default: 1.0).

vip.usage_tips: It receives X and y directly — there is no need to run a PLS beforehand, the block trains its own. Use `selected_indices` to crop X (with `selecao_variaveis`) and retrain the PLS with fewer variables. To avoid information leakage, compute the VIP using only the training set.

vip_interpretation.description: PLS VIP scores with analysis of the most important regions.

wavelet_transform.description: Discrete wavelet decomposition for smoothing, decomposition or feature extraction.
